subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Check the continuity of the function f given by f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x² − 2x − 3) for 0 < x < 5 and x ≠ 3, and f(3) = 1.5, at the point x = 3.

mark_split.label: Factorise the numerator and the denominator

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.189, chapter 8 LIMITS AND CONTINUITY, the CONTINUITY sub-section, Short Answer question 3. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints a CHAPTER-level marks banner (4 Marks over this CONTINUITY sub-section) but no per-step allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 shape follows the shape this bank uses for a Maths-1B Section B question. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. Paper position: Maths-1B Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. ⚠ THE PRINTED STEM IS DEFECTIVE IN TWO WAYS, AND BOTH ARE REPAIRED HERE, NOT SILENTLY. (1) BRACKETS: the book prints the function as (x² − 9)/x² − 2x − 3), with an unmatched closing bracket and no opening bracket around the denominator. Read literally that is (x² − 9)/x² − 2x − 3, a different function. The reading authored here is the denominator (x² − 2x − 3). (2) THE POINT: the book never names the point at which continuity is to be tested. The point authored here is x = 3. Both repairs are self-confirming from the book's own data: (x² − 9)/(x² − 2x − 3) = (x − 3)(x + 3)/[(x − 3)(x + 1)] = (x + 3)/(x + 1), which is exactly 6/4 = 1.5 at x = 3 — the value the book itself assigns to f(3). A stem whose given f(3) equals the limit of the bracketed reading at x = 3 can only be that reading tested at that point. Note also that x = 3 is the only point of the stated domain 0 < x < 5 where the denominator vanishes: its other root, x = −1, lies outside that interval, which is why the domain is stated as it is.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say why you cannot just substitute 3, and what you would do to the numerator and the denominator first.

steps.label: State the continuity test at 3
steps.margin_note: First mark. Say the test, and say why substitution alone will not give the limit: at x = 3 the numerator and the denominator are both 0, which is the indeterminate form 0/0.
steps.memory_tip: A rational function that gives 0/0 at a point has (x − that point) as a factor of both the top and the bottom — that is the same statement as the factor theorem.
lines: Given f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x² − 2x − 3)   for 0 < x < 5, x ≠ 3,   and f(3) = 1.5
f is continuous at x = 3 if   lim(x → 3) f(x) = f(3)
So direct substitution gives 0/0, an indeterminate form, and the limit must be worked out.

recall.must_convey: That continuity at 3 means lim(x → 3) f(x) must equal f(3), and that substituting 3 gives 0/0.
accept: continuity at three means the limit equals f of three
putting three gives zero by zero so the limit has to be worked
state the test then find the limit at three
three substitute cheste zero by zero vasthundi
check whether the limit at three is one point five

steps.why: Recording that both the top and the bottom are 0 at x = 3 is what justifies factorising rather than substituting, and it is the line that earns this mark.
common_mistakes: Writing the limit as 0/0 and calling it the answer.
Saying f is not continuous because f is undefined at 3 in the first formula, when f(3) is separately given.

steps.label: Factorise the numerator and the denominator
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both factorisations must show the common factor (x − 3). Splitting the middle term −2x as −3x + x is the quickest route for the denominator.
steps.memory_tip: For x² − 2x − 3 look for two numbers with product −3 and sum −2: they are −3 and +1, so the factors are (x − 3)(x + 1).

recall.must_convey: That x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3) and x² − 2x − 3 = (x − 3)(x + 1), so (x − 3) is a common factor.
accept: factorise both, x minus three is common to top and bottom
x squared minus nine is x minus three into x plus three
x squared minus two x minus three is x minus three into x plus one
rendintini factorise cheste x minus three common ga vasthundi
split the middle term to factorise the denominator
heard_as: x minus three into x plus three
x minus three into x plus one

steps.why: The 0/0 form says (x − 3) divides both the numerator and the denominator, so factorising is guaranteed to produce it. This is the step that removes the source of the indeterminate form.
common_mistakes: Factorising x² − 2x − 3 as (x + 3)(x − 1), which multiplies out to x² + 2x − 3.

steps.label: Cancel and take the limit
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The cancellation is legal only because x ≠ 3 inside a limit at 3 — the limit never uses the value at the point itself. After cancelling, the value can simply be substituted.
steps.memory_tip: In lim(x → 3), x is near 3 but never equal to 3, so a factor of (x − 3) is never zero and may be cancelled.
lines: In lim(x → 3), x is close to 3 but x ≠ 3, so (x − 3) ≠ 0 and it cancels:
The remaining denominator x + 1 is 0 only at x = −1, which is outside 0 < x < 5

recall.must_convey: That (x − 3) cancels because x ≠ 3 in the limit, leaving (x + 3)/(x + 1), whose value at 3 is 6/4 = 1.5.
accept: cancel x minus three and substitute to get six by four
after cancelling it is x plus three over x plus one which is one point five at three
in the limit x is not equal to three so the factor cancels
x minus three cancel chesi three substitute cheste six by four
the limit is six by four that is one point five
heard_as: x plus three by x plus one

steps.why: A limit at 3 depends only on values near 3, never on the value at 3 itself, so cancelling a factor that is zero only at 3 changes nothing about the limit.
common_mistakes: Refusing to cancel because (x − 3) is 0 at x = 3, when the limit never uses that point.
Writing 6/4 as 1.2 or leaving it unsimplified when the given f(3) is a decimal.

steps.label: Compare with f(3) and conclude
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The comparison line must be written out. Note that 6/4 and 1.5 are the same number written two ways — say so, rather than leaving the reader to check it.
steps.memory_tip: Write the limit and the value side by side in one line before the conclusion — the examiner is looking for exactly that comparison.

recall.must_convey: That the limit 1.5 equals the given f(3) = 1.5, so f is continuous at 3.
accept: the limit is one point five and f of three is one point five so it is continuous
six by four is one point five which matches the given value
limit and value are equal so f is continuous at three
limit and f of three rendu one point five, so continuous
yes it is continuous at x equals three

steps.why: The value f(3) = 1.5 was chosen precisely to close the gap the first formula leaves open, so the comparison is what shows the definition of continuity is met.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the limit without comparing it with the given f(3).
Reporting the answer as 3/2 without noting that the given value 1.5 is the same number.

insider_note: Both top and bottom vanish at 3, so factorise both and cancel the shared (x − 3). The surviving (x + 3)/(x + 1) gives 1.5, matching the given f(3) exactly.
